extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and general readers interested in literature and cultural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles from G. K. Chesterton's Heretics for judging literature, politics, and moral discourse — emphasising the role of doctrine, idealism, and imaginative interest. Useful for critics or writers who want criteria for what makes literary or political work substantial rather than merely fashionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of a man's view of the universe
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the most practical and important thing about a man is still his view of the universe.’ A writer's or person's ultimate philosophy (religion, doctrine, cosmic theory) is more important than incidental facts about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate authors and public figures by the coherence and practical consequences of their underlying philosophy; consider whether their stated worldview informs action and public life. Chesterton contrasts knowing someone's income with knowing his philosophy (landlady/lodger) and a general's need to know the enemy's philosophy rather than mere numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of generalizations and doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: General theories and the habit of generalizing (orthodoxy) are necessary; modern dismissal of grand theories leads to triviality and ineffectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that propose and defend broad principles rather than those that merely catalogue particulars. Chesterton argues that discarding generalizations in favour of detail (‘The golden rule is that there is no golden rule’) leads to an inability to act decisively or to understand ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature should present ideals not only expose evils
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern realism tends to have a 'certain vagueness ... towards what is really wisdom and virtue' and often shows only knowledge of evil; by contrast literature ought to supply vivid images of good, perfection, and improvement (Heaven, Purgatory, Hell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing fiction or drama, check whether the work supplies a positive moral or ideal (a vision of what is good) rather than only diagnosing social ills; Chesterton contrasts Dante's tripartite moral vision with Ibsen's focus on hell or failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of 'art for art's sake' and mere aestheticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The extrusion of general ideals from art ('art for art's sake') impoverishes literature; art divorced from moral/philosophical aims tends to produce trivial or smaller results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge art by whether it engages with moral/philosophical questions and aims, not merely by technical virtuosity or novelty. Chesterton contends that when literature abandons general ideals, it produces 'a race of small men in the arts.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of prioritizing efficiency and opportunism
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern cry of 'efficiency' and opportunism (politics for politics' sake) replaces ideals and yields mediocre, short-sighted outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political and social writing for fidelity to enduring aims rather than transient efficiency; be skeptical of solutions that focus on process without defining ends. Chesterton uses Lord Rosebery as symbol of opportunism's failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blasphemy as an artistic effect requires conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Blasphemy 'is an artistic effect, because blasphemy depends upon a philosophical conviction.' Genuine irreverence presupposes belief; irreverence without conviction is hollow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a work seeks shock or sacrilege, ask whether it springs from coherent conviction; hollow provocation is less artistically effective. Example: Milton's Satan has grandeur because of theological grounding, whereas rash blasphemy will soon exhaust itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism without idealism is inadequate and potentially harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Realists like Zola or Ibsen, by concentrating on exposing evil, often leave no clear image of good and thus act like 'Terrorists'—they may promote morality only in a limited, fear-driven way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware works that use stark realism or shock to promote morality without proposing positive ideals; these may affect only a small minority and can even desensitise or thrill rather than ennoble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress requires a prior moral definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'progress' is meaningless without a previously defined moral doctrine; one cannot measure or advocate progress without specifying the direction or ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proposals for reform or 'progress' by checking whether the author defines what counts as better; treat appeals to progress without doctrine as evasions. Chesterton argues progress must presuppose a creed or code of morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with fundamentals/theories before addressing processes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'far more practical to begin at the beginning and discuss theories.' Addressing policies or processes without settling underlying definitions (e.g., what is liberty, religion) is futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In essays and political argument, require clear statement of first principles before policy recommendations; Chesterton prefers doctrinal clarity (thirteenth-century scholastic methods) to muddled opportunism.

rubrics_metrics.name: A strong philosophy produces stronger practical men
rubrics_metrics.description: Men dominated by a philosophy or religion produced big results historically; bondage to doctrine often yielded more effective action than modern 'freedom' without conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works that show a fusion of belief and action; when judging historical or political narratives, give weight to the presence of motivating doctrines that led to coherent action (e.g., Hildebrand, Danton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism must not dismiss cosmic philosophy as irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern habit of saying 'his philosophy does not matter' is mistaken: cosmic theories shape practical life and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating character, policy, or art, consider the practical consequences of the subject's philosophical commitments; Chesterton gives examples (conversational pessimist leading to social inversion) to show theory's effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrinal clarity is preferable to fashionable 'liberty' that avoids decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern 'liberty' often means avoiding decisions about what is good; this dodge prevents moral articulation and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize appeals to tolerance or liberty that function to avoid moral judgment; prefer authors who risk doctrinal claims rather than those who hide behind amorphous freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find poetry in common subjects; interest—not subject—makes poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There is no such thing on earth as an uninteresting subject; the only thing that can exist is an uninterested person.’ Common things can be poetical if the writer is interested and imaginative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess descriptive writing by the writer's capacity to invest ordinary objects and trades with vividness and wonder (Chesterton's example: the smith as poetical). A lack of interest, not a dull subject, produces boredom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evocative, meaningful names and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and symbols that connect to history, trade, or archetype (e.g., 'Smith') enrich character and poetry; meaningless names weaken resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or evaluating fiction, prefer nomenclature and symbolic details that evoke larger traditions or elemental qualities rather than arbitrary or vacuous names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral imagination (vision of perfection) is wholesome
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystic or visionary religion is 'necessarily more wholesome' than a morality that only contemplates imperfection; the mystic fixes thoughts on 'gigantic strength and happiness' even if it leads to personal eccentricity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value literature and moral writing that supply vivid, affirmative pictures of wholeness and happiness (even idealised) because they foster wholesome aspiration; contrast this with moralities constituted solely by warnings and images of disease (the 'drunkard's liver').
